import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Rota's basis conjecture

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rota%27s_basis_conjecture)
-/

namespace RotasBasisConjecture

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture.** For every rank-$n$ matroid and every family of $n$
pairwise disjoint bases $B_i$, the elements can be arranged in an $n \times n$ matrix
whose $i$-th row is exactly $B_i$ and each of whose columns is also a base.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (α : Type*) (M : Matroid α) (B : Fin n → Set α),
      M.eRank = n →
      (∀ i, M.IsBase (B i)) →
      Set.univ.PairwiseDisjoint B →
      ∃ A : Fin n → Fin n → α,
        Function.Injective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n ↦ A p.1 p.2) ∧
        (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧
        ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i ↦ A i j) := by
  sorry

end RotasBasisConjecture
modeling_decisions: Used Mathlib's `Matroid.eRank : ℕ∞` with `M.eRank = n` (via the natural-number coercion) to express that the matroid has finite rank exactly `n`.

Represented the arrangement directly as a matrix `A : Fin n → Fin n → α`. For each row, equality of its range with `B i` says that the row is exactly the prescribed base; global injectivity makes the arrangement explicitly use every element without repetition.
Represented each column as `Set.range (fun i ↦ A i j)` and required this set to satisfy `M.IsBase`.
Used `Set.univ.PairwiseDisjoint B` for pairwise disjointness of the `Fin n`-indexed input bases.
Allowed `n = 0`; all matrix conditions are then vacuous and the conjecture has the intended trivial boundary case.
Formalized the general matroid version from the background article, rather than only its vector-space special case.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Rota's basis conjecture

Rota's basis conjecture states that if $M$ is a matroid of rank $n$ (for example a vector
space of dimension $n$) and $B_1, \dots, B_n$ are $n$ pairwise disjoint bases of $M$, then
the elements of these bases can be arranged into an $n \times n$ matrix whose $i$-th row
consists exactly of the elements of $B_i$ and whose columns are also bases of $M$.
Equivalently, there are $n$ disjoint bases $C_1, \dots, C_n$ of $M$, each of which consists of
one element from each of the bases $B_i$.

The conjecture was first published by Huang and Rota (1994), who credit it to Rota (1989).
It is known for $n \le 3$ and for paving matroids, but it is open in general.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Rota's basis conjecture*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rota%27s_basis_conjecture)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. Huang and G.-C. Rota, *On the relations of various conjectures on Latin squares and
  straightening coefficients*, Discrete Mathematics **128** (1994),
  225–236](https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(94)90114-7)
-/

open Function

namespace RotasBasisConjecture

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture**

Let $M$ be a matroid of rank $n$ and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be $n$ pairwise disjoint bases
of $M$. Then there is an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ such that, for every $i$, the entries of the
$i$-th row of $A$ are exactly the elements of $B_i$, and, for every $j$, the entries of the
$j$-th column of $A$ form a base of $M$.

The rank of $M$ is `Matroid.eRank`, so `M.eRank = n` says that every base of $M$ is finite
with exactly $n$ elements. In particular `Set.range (A i) = B i` says that the $i$-th row
of $A$ lists the $n$ elements of $B_i$ without repetition, and every column of $A$ is then a base
of $M$ containing exactly one element of each $B_i$. The case $n = 0$ is trivially true.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 15]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture {α : Type*} (M : Matroid α) (n : ℕ) (hM : M.eRank = n)
    (B : Fin n → Set α) (hB : ∀ i, M.IsBase (B i)) (hdisj : Pairwise (Disjoint on B)) :
    ∃ A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧ ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j) := by
  sorry

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture for vector spaces**

Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n$ over a field $K$ and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be
$n$ pairwise disjoint bases of $V$. Then there is an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with entries in $V$
such that, for every $i$, the entries of the $i$-th row of $A$ are exactly the vectors of $B_i$,
and, for every $j$, the entries of the $j$-th column of $A$ form a basis of $V$.

This is the special case of `rotas_basis_conjecture` for the linear matroid of $V$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 15]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture.variants.vectorSpace {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V]
    [Module K V] [Module.Finite K V] (n : ℕ) (hV : Module.finrank K V = n)
    (B : Fin n → Module.Basis (Fin n) K V)
    (hdisj : Pairwise (Disjoint on fun i => Set.range (B i))) :
    ∃ A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) V,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = Set.range (B i)) ∧
        ∀ j, ∃ C : Module.Basis (Fin n) K V, ⇑C = fun i => A i j := by
  sorry

/--
Sanity check: for $n = 0$ there are no bases to arrange and no columns to check,
so the conjecture holds trivially.
-/
@[category test, AMS 5 15]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture.variants.zero {α : Type*} (M : Matroid α) (_hM : M.eRank = 0)
    (B : Fin 0 → Set α) (_hB : ∀ i, M.IsBase (B i)) (_hdisj : Pairwise (Disjoint on B)) :
    ∃ A : Matrix (Fin 0) (Fin 0) α,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧ ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j) :=
  ⟨Matrix.of fun i => i.elim0, fun i => i.elim0, fun j => j.elim0⟩

end RotasBasisConjecture
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single-slot decomposition matches the statement; the n = 0 boundary case and the vector-space special case are handled as described in the notes.
modeling_decisions: 'Matroid of rank n' is rendered as `M.eRank = (n : ℕ∞)` because this Mathlib version has only the ℕ∞-valued `Matroid.eRank` (no ℕ-valued rank). By `Matroid.IsBase.encard_eq_eRank` this forces every base to be finite with exactly n elements, so finite rank is implied and no separate `RankFinite` hypothesis is needed.

The n×n matrix is `A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α`; 'rows are B_i' is `Set.range (A i) = B i`. Since |B_i| = n and a row has n positions, this forces each row to enumerate B_i bijectively (no repeated entries), matching 'arrange the elements of these bases'.

'Columns are also bases' is `M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j)`; because every entry of row i lies in B_i and the B_i are disjoint, each column automatically contains exactly one element of every B_i, which is the article's equivalent 'transversal bases C_i' formulation.
'n disjoint bases' is read as pairwise disjoint (`Pairwise (Disjoint on B)` with `open Function` for the `on` notation), indexed by `Fin n`; distinct indices give disjoint hence distinct bases.
Bases are `Set α` (Mathlib's matroid convention), not `Finset`; finiteness follows from the rank hypothesis.
n = 0 is allowed and is trivially true (Fin 0 is empty); this is recorded by a `category test` declaration `rotas_basis_conjecture.variants.zero` with a one-line proof.

Added an extra open variant `rotas_basis_conjecture.variants.vectorSpace` for the vector-space form explicitly mentioned in the article ('if X is either a vector space of dimension n or more generally a matroid of rank n'): V a finite-dimensional K-vector space with `Module.finrank K V = n`, bases as `Module.Basis (Fin n) K V` with pairwise disjoint ranges, rows have the same range as B_i, and each column is (the coercion of) some `Module.Basis (Fin n) K V`. The hypotheses `[Module.Finite K V]` and `hV` are partly redundant with the existence of the bases B_i but are kept to mirror the phrase 'vector space of dimension n'. This variant is background per the decomposition notes and is not the slot declaration.
AMS tags `5 15` (combinatorics for matroids, linear algebra for the vector-space form), in ascending order.

rotas_basis_conjecture.why: Stated with Mathlib's `Matroid`: for every type α, matroid `M : Matroid α`, `n : ℕ` with `M.eRank = n`, and `B : Fin n → Set α` with each `M.IsBase (B i)` and `Pairwise (Disjoint on B)`, there exists `A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α` with `Set.range (A i) = B i` for every row `i` and `M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j)` for every column `j`. Existing primitives (`Matroid.eRank`, `Matroid.IsBase`, `Matrix`, `Set.range`, `Pairwise`/`Disjoint on`) suffice; no new definitions.

/-!

bases $B_1, \dots, B_n$, then it is possible to arrange the elements of these bases into an
$n \times n$ matrix in such a way that the rows of the matrix are exactly the given bases and the
columns of the matrix are also bases of $M$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Rota's basis conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rota%27s_basis_conjecture)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. Huang, G.-C. Rota, *On the relations of various conjectures on Latin squares and

namespace RotasBasisConjecture

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture.** Let $M$ be a matroid of rank $n$ and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be $n$
pairwise disjoint bases of $M$. Then the elements of these bases can be arranged into an
$n \times n$ matrix whose $i$-th row is exactly the base $B_i$ (for every $i$) and each of whose
columns is also a base of $M$.

Equivalently, there are $n$ disjoint bases $C_1, \dots, C_n$ of $M$ (the columns), each
consisting of exactly one element from each of the bases $B_1, \dots, B_n$.

Here the matrix is `A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α`, with `i`-th row `A i` and `j`-th column
`fun i ↦ A i j`. Every base of `M` has exactly `n` elements, so `Set.range (A i) = B i` says that
the `i`-th row lists the elements of `B i` without repetition, and the disjointness of the `B i`
then says that the entries of `A` are exactly the elements of `B 1, …, B n`.
The case `n = 0` is trivially true.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 15]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture {α : Type*} (n : ℕ) (M : Matroid α) (hM : M.eRank = n)
    (B : Fin n → Set α) (hB : ∀ i, M.IsBase (B i))
    (hdisj : Pairwise fun i j ↦ Disjoint (B i) (B j)) :
    ∃ A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧ ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i ↦ A i j) := by

end RotasBasisConjecture
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single-slot decomposition matches the list entry; the vector-space form is the linear-matroid special case and is correctly treated as background.
modeling_decisions: Matroids are Mathlib's `Matroid α` (possibly infinite ground set, defined via bases). 'Rank n' is encoded as `M.eRank = (n : ℕ∞)`, which forces all bases to be finite of cardinality exactly n (`Matroid.IsBase.encard_eq_eRank`). No ℕ-valued `Matroid.rank` exists in this Mathlib version.
The n×n matrix is `A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α` (definitionally `Fin n → Fin n → α`); row i is `A i`, column j is `fun i ↦ A i j`.

'Rows are B_i' is encoded as `Set.range (A i) = B i`. /-!
# Rota's basis conjecture

Let $M$ be a matroid of rank $n$ (or, as a special case, a vector space of dimension $n$)
and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be $n$ pairwise disjoint bases of $M$. Rota's basis conjecture
states that the $n^2$ elements of these bases can be arranged into an $n \times n$ matrix
whose $i$-th row consists exactly of the elements of $B_i$ and whose $n$ columns are all
bases of $M$. Equivalently, there are $n$ disjoint bases $C_1, \dots, C_n$ of $M$, each
consisting of exactly one element from each $B_i$.

The conjecture was first published by Huang and Rota (1994), who credit it to Rota (1989).
It is known for $n \le 3$ (Chan, 1995) and for paving matroids (Geelen and Humphries, 2006),
but it is open in general, even for vector spaces.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Rota's basis conjecture*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rota%27s_basis_conjecture)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. Huang and G.-C. Rota, *On the relations of various conjectures on Latin squares and
  straightening coefficients*, Discrete Mathematics **128** (1994),
  225–236](https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(94)90114-7)
- [W. Chan, *An exchange property of matroid*, Discrete Mathematics **146** (1995),
  299–302](https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(94)00071-3)
-/

namespace RotasBasisConjecture

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture.**

Let $M$ be a matroid of rank $n$ and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be $n$ pairwise disjoint bases
of $M$. Then it is possible to arrange the elements of $B_1, \dots, B_n$ into an
$n \times n$ matrix $A$ such that the $i$-th row of $A$ consists exactly of the elements
of $B_i$ and every column of $A$ is a base of $M$.

Here the rank of $M$ is `M.eRank : ℕ∞`, so the hypothesis `M.eRank = n` says that $M$ has
finite rank $n$; in particular every base of $M$ has exactly $n$ elements. The matrix is a
function `A : Fin n → Fin n → α`, where `A i j` is the entry in row $i$ and column $j$; the
row condition `Set.range (A i) = B i` forces each row to list the $n$ elements of $B_i$
without repetition.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 15]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture {α : Type*} (n : ℕ) (M : Matroid α) (hM : M.eRank = n)
    (B : Fin n → Set α) (hB : ∀ i, M.IsBase (B i))
    (hdisj : Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (B i) (B j)) :
    ∃ A : Fin n → Fin n → α,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧ ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j) := by
  sorry

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture for vector spaces.**

Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n$ over a field $K$ and let $b_1, \dots, b_n$ be $n$
bases of $V$ with pairwise disjoint underlying sets of vectors. Then the $n^2$ vectors can be
arranged into an $n \times n$ matrix whose $i$-th row consists exactly of the vectors of
$b_i$ and whose columns are all bases of $V$.

This is the special case of `rotas_basis_conjecture` for linear matroids. Each basis is
indexed by `Fin n`, so $V$ automatically has dimension $n$; a column of $n$ vectors is then
a basis of $V$ if and only if it is linearly independent.
-/

theorem rotas_basis_conjecture.variants.vectorSpace {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V]
    [Module K V] (n : ℕ) (b : Fin n → Module.Basis (Fin n) K V)

    ∃ A : Fin n → Fin n → V,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = Set.range (b i)) ∧ ∀ j, LinearIndependent K fun i => A i j := by

/--
Rota's basis conjecture holds for all matroids of rank $n \le 3$. The case $n = 3$ is due
to Chan (1995); the cases $n \le 2$ are elementary.

[W. Chan, *An exchange property of matroid*, Discrete Mathematics **146** (1995), 299–302.]
-/

    ∃ A : Fin n → Fin n → α,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧ ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j) := by

end RotasBasisConjecture
